Here's my perspective on tradition: anything that was true or valuable in the past and is still true or valuable now should be discoverable as such, now, and rationally--without appealing to tradition. If a thing wasn't true or wasn't valuable in the past, we have no reason to think it is now; but, if a thing that wasn't true or valuable became true and/or valuable, that fact should be discoverable as such, now, and rationally as well.

Nationalism: Always a solid choice. Well done.

The first thing I would say is that those who want to stick with tradition are rarely talking about technology and the use of physical objects, and instead are more focused on social and cultural aspects of life.

You'll be hard pressed to find the individual who would rather spend weeks plowing the same field he could plow in an afternoon using modern machinery. This isn't always the case, nor should it be. There are indeed times where the old ways may be better or at very least more pleasing; there's a reason we hold a higher value for something that is hand made. It is also worth noting that in our push to create machines that do the amazing things they are capable of, we have created a looming natural disaster that at some point in the fairly near future (100-300 years) is going to bite us in the ass, and hard. That line of thinking gets a little muddy as you have to accept that the rapid rate of technological improvement lead us to the techniques and instruments needed to detect the damage in the first place, so it becomes a little 'chicken or the egg'. The main takeaway would be that unbridled technological development isn't purely good and can have drawbacks, even if they are often outweighed by the positive aspects of whatever is created. All in all however, most are of the mindset that technological development is a net positive for society.

So, that would leave us with social and cultural. Here, traditions work to hold a society together by emphasizing common values and pastimes of generally great importance to a society; ones that likely aren't celebrated by other peoples, at least not in the same way.

At times these traditions can be ritualistic in a way, and may even be superstitious in origin, but that isn't inherently a bad thing. For a small example let's look at Christmas. I'm from the US, so my familiarity with the event comes from that perspective. It's a holiday based on a religious tradition, so there's your 'superstitious'. It has a date, and while the precise timing and style of that date may change between families, it is often done the same way year to year, so ritualistic in a way.

This is where traditions can have bonding element to them. The date's purpose is generally known, and the stories that are most commonly repeated and most timeless are the ones that focus on values we can share with one another. By highlighting common values between us, we can more readily identify those who are our people as opposed to those who are the 'others'. It's one reason that there's a feather-wrinkling every year about that 'You can't even say Merry Christmas anymore' stuff; you're shitting on far more than the symbolic birthday for a religious deity, and the more people try and brush it off as unimportant, the more that resentment grows.

You might even be able to take it a step further. We don't simply stop looking to commonalities between our fellow man, we just try and adjust to what that commonality is. Look at the Social Justice movement-thing we face. Why in the hell has something so toxic to most become the generally accepted 'norm' these days? I would say that it was the only thing that could possibly connect the otherwise un-connectable peoples of a 'multicultural' society. The name says it in itself; there is no longer a shared culture and in turn no shared cultural value. So we filled the void of a bond with our neighbors with a high-minded ideology that in private, once we get amongst our own, we trash as unreliable nonsense.

So in short I would say that tradition doesn't interfere with innovation, but stands clear of it while enhancing the bond we have with our form of civilization and those who similarly hold it in high esteem.
